title: How To Earn Back The Trust Of A Student You’ve Hurt Or Disappointed uve-hurt-or-disappointed/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Prompted by a story of a teacher who wrongly accused a student of misbehavior and lost her temper, Linsin lays out a five-step process for repairing the relationship: being genuinely serious rather than glossing over the incident, apologizing directly without justifying or explaining yourself, explicitly taking responsibility with a brief "I'm sorry," moving on without waiting around for the student to formally accept the apology, and not bringing the incident up again afterward. He argues that pressuring a student for acceptance actually undermines genuine forgiveness, while a clean, no-strings apology followed by moving forward makes it more likely to be accepted. He closes by framing a teacher's willingness to own mistakes as a model of accountability for students and as something that builds humility, mindfulness, and integrity in the teacher over time.
points: A five-step repair process after wrongly hurting a student: be real, be direct, take responsibility, move on, and don't mention it again.
Apologies should come with no strings attached — explaining or justifying your actions weakens the apology's impact.
Don't wait around for the student to formally accept the apology; pressuring for acceptance can undermine genuine forgiveness.
A teacher's willingness to own mistakes models accountability for students and builds humility and integrity in the teacher.
quotes: The problem—besides making several critical accountability errors—was that she got it wrong.
It’s best to pull the student aside, look them in the eye, and apologize.
It’s a mistake to be lighthearted or overly friendly with the student you’ve hurt or disappointed.
An apology is the only honest and reliable way to erase any resentment the student may be feeling toward you. But it must come with no strings attached.
To that end, admit that you messed up, that you handled it poorly or shouldn’t have said what you said. Take no more than 30 seconds, and then say the critical words: “I’m sorry.
Students—and people in general—are more likely to accept an apology, and therefore truly forgive, when there is no pressure for them to do so.
By confessing our mistakes, by apologizing when we’re wrong and taking responsibility when we hurt others, we become better people and better teachers.
